conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___, the neurology team. I understand you came in with some dizziness and trouble finding words earlier today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I woke up at 4:30 this morning feeling like the room was spinning. Objects seemed to be moving. I’ve never felt quite like that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned some word-finding difficulty when you were in the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. When I was trying to tell the nurse my medical history, I just couldn’t pull up the words. It scared me. But it got better after a few minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good it improved. The fact that it came on suddenly and you have a history of TIAs makes us want to be very careful. We’ve already done a CT scan of your head to rule out a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had four TIAs before, all about a year ago. But this feels different. More like vertigo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right. The spinning sensation, worse when you move your head or sit up, is classic for vertigo. But because of your history, we need to be sure it’s not a new stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve been feeling weak and tired for about a week. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. That could suggest a viral illness. Sometimes a virus can affect the inner ear and cause vertigo—what we call viral vestibulopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not a stroke?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan came back normal—no bleeding or stroke. But we’ll do an MRI later today for a more detailed look. We also did a chest X-ray since you have a pacemaker, to make sure it’s safe for the MRI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. My pacemaker is MRI-incompatible. But I walked across the street fine earlier. I’m still a bit unsteady, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your Romberg test showed some sway, which fits with vertigo. We’ll keep you lying down for now and avoid sudden movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my medications? I take apixaban for atrial fibrillation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your apixaban. Given your history, we also started aspirin temporarily until we rule out stroke. Once the MRI is clear, we’ll stop the aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds—amlodipine and clonidine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held those for now. Your blood pressure is stable, and we don’t want to drop it too low if your symptoms are related to blood flow issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my testosterone shot? I usually get it weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding that for now. Since you’ve been feeling unwell, it’s safer to delay it until you’re more stable. You’ll follow up with endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fair enough. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling an MRI of your brain and neck with contrast. We also ordered one of your cervical spine and pituitary, just to be thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pituitary? Because of the vision changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You mentioned spatial disorientation and past vision issues. We want to rule out any mass or structural cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mitochondrial disease—could that be playing a role?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Your body doesn’t handle stress well—like infections or metabolic changes. This could be a viral trigger on top of your autonomic dysfunction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had worse tinnitus lately too. And my hearing’s always been worse on the right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. The vertigo could be related to your inner ear. The MRI will help assess the vestibular nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’ve reviewed your MRI results. The good news is: no stroke, no bleed, no tumor. Your brain and blood vessels look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So what is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely viral vestibulopathy. The fact that you felt unwell a week before, plus the vertigo and no other neurological deficits, points to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the word-finding issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could have been a brief episode of brain fog from the vertigo or mild cerebral hypoperfusion. But no stroke signs. Your exam today shows only mild difficulty with word recall—much better than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the spine MRI? I have a lot of neck arthritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have degenerative changes, especially at C4-C5, but no spinal cord compression or new lesions. It’s stable compared to your last scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pituitary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Normal. No mass or abnormality. So we can rule that out as a cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll restart your blood pressure meds—amlodipine and clonidine. Continue apixaban. And you can resume your testosterone shot with your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy for a few days. Avoid sudden head movements. If the dizziness worsens or you develop new symptoms—like weakness, vision loss, or slurred speech—come back immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send a note to your primary doctor and neurologist. Follow up with them in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The room isn’t spinning as much. I walked down the hall without help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your gait is steady, and your coordination has improved. We’re comfortable sending you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep taking all my meds as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly as prescribed. And stay hydrated—important with your mitochondrial condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I be worried about another TIA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your risk factors are well-managed—on apixaban, blood pressure controlled. This episode doesn’t look like a TIA, but always be alert to new symptoms. You’re doing well.
